chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The time of Fajr (dawn prayer) is when the dawn breaks until the morning light covers the sky, and it is not proper to delay it intentionally, but it is the time for one who is busy or forgetful or asleep.

key_terms.الصُّبْحُ: Morning; the period of early morning light.
key_terms.الْفَجْرُ: Dawn; the time of the first light before sunrise, specifically referring to the prayer time.
key_terms.تَأْخِيرُ: Delaying; putting off the prayer from its optimal time.
key_terms.لِمَنْ شُغِلَ: For one who is busy; a justification for delayed prayer due to valid reasons.
key_terms.يَتَجَلَّلَ: Covers or envelops; referring to the full illumination of the sky by morning light.
key_terms.يَنْشَقُّ: Breaks or splits; referring to the emergence of dawn light.

ai.seo_question: What is the defined time range for the Fajr prayer in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) delineates the Fajr prayer window, distinguishing between the primary time (from first light to full sunrise glow) and the secondary time for those excused by busyness, forgetfulness, or sleep. It underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on *ibtida'* (commencement) of the time while maintaining the preference for timely performance, reflecting the balance between strict adherence and practical ease in ritual law.
